title: Water Resources
subject: geography
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Geography: 17 marks + 3 map marks). Map work from this chapter: dams (Salal, Bhakra Nangal, Tehri, Rana Pratap Sagar, Sardar Sarovar, Hirakud, Nagarjuna Sagar, Tungabhadra). Map items are given here as text questions.

sections.title: Water everywhere, not a drop to drink?

blocks.title: Why is a rainy city short of water?
blocks.body:
Shillong in Meghalaya is only about **55 km** from Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, among the wettest places on Earth. Yet nearly every house in Shillong collects rain from its roof, because the city still runs short of water.

Water is renewable, yet India faces scarcity. How can that be? This chapter explains why water becomes scarce, how big dams try to solve the problem and create new ones, and how people across India have harvested rain for centuries.

blocks.title: The waterman of India
blocks.body:
In the 1980s, Rajendra Singh began helping villagers in the dry Alwar district of Rajasthan to revive old **johads**, small earthen check dams that catch rainwater. Wells filled again, and rivers that had dried up, like the **Arvari**, began to flow.

His organisation, Tarun Bharat Sangh, helped build thousands of johads. In 2015 he received the Stockholm Water Prize. His work shows that traditional wisdom can solve modern water problems.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in hydrology, civil and water engineering, environmental planning and rural development.

blocks.question: Water is renewed by the water cycle. Why, then, does India face water scarcity?
options: Over-use and unequal access by a large population, plus pollution
Because it never rains in India
Because water is a non-renewable resource
blocks.explanation: Scarcity is mostly caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access, not by a lack of rain alone.

blocks.title: Why water becomes scarce
blocks.body:
Three-fourths of the Earth's surface is covered with water, but only a small proportion is **freshwater** that can be used. Freshwater comes mainly from **surface runoff and groundwater**, continually renewed and recharged through the **hydrological cycle**. About **96.5 per cent** of the world's water is in the oceans and only **2.5 per cent** is freshwater; nearly **70 per cent** of this freshwater is locked in ice sheets and glaciers, and a little less than **30 per cent** is stored as groundwater.

Water is a renewable resource, but **water scarcity** can arise even in areas with plenty of rain or rivers. Its causes:
- **Large and growing population:** more water for domestic use and more food grown.
- **Irrigated agriculture:** to grow more food, water resources are over-exploited for irrigation and for **dry-season agriculture**.
- **Over-use of groundwater:** many farmers have their own wells and tube-wells, which leads to falling groundwater levels.
- **Industrialisation and urbanisation:** industries need water and also electricity, much of it from **hydroelectric power**; cities with large populations and urban lifestyles add to the demand, and housing societies often have their own groundwater pumps.
- **Unequal access** among social groups.
- **Poor quality of water:** even where water is available, it may be **polluted** by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, making it unfit for use.

So we need to **conserve and manage** water: to safeguard ourselves from health hazards, ensure food security, continue our livelihoods and productive activities, and prevent the degradation of natural ecosystems. Over-exploitation and mismanagement may impoverish this resource and cause ecological crisis.

blocks.question: What share of the world's water is freshwater?
blocks.explanation: Only about 2.5 per cent of the Earth's water is freshwater.
option_feedback: 70 per cent of freshwater is ice.
Under 30 per cent of freshwater is groundwater.

blocks.question: Which is NOT a cause of water scarcity in India?
options: Lack of any rainfall in the country
blocks.explanation: Scarcity is caused by over-use, unequal access and pollution, even in areas that get rain.

blocks.title: Ancient hydraulic works and multipurpose projects
blocks.body:
**Hydraulic structures in ancient India:**
- In the **1st century BC**, **Sringaverapura near Prayagraj (Allahabad)** had a sophisticated water harvesting system channelling the flood water of the **Ganga**.
- During **Chandragupta Maurya's** time, dams, lakes and irrigation systems were extensively built.
- Evidence of sophisticated irrigation works has been found in **Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra)**.
- In the **11th century**, **Bhopal Lake**, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built.
- In the **14th century**, the tank in **Hauz Khas, Delhi**, was constructed by **Iltutmish** to supply water to the **Siri Fort** area.

**Dams:** a dam is a **barrier across flowing water** that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a **reservoir, lake or impoundment**. 'Dam' usually refers to the reservoir rather than the structure. Most dams have a section called a **spillway or weir** over which, or through which, water flows. Dams are classified by **structure and materials** (timber dams, embankment dams, masonry dams) and by **height** (large or major dams; low, medium and high dams).

**Multipurpose river projects:** dams today are built not just for irrigation but for **electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial uses, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding**. For example, in the **Sutlej-Beas** basin, the **Bhakra-Nangal** project water is used both for **hydel power and irrigation**; the **Hirakud** project in the **Mahanadi** basin integrates **conservation of water with flood control**. Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the **'temples of modern India'**, because they would integrate agriculture, the village economy, rapid industrialisation and growth of the urban economy.

**Why dams are opposed:**
- Regulating and damming rivers affects their **natural flow**, causing **poor sediment flow** and **excessive sedimentation** at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting in **rockier stream beds** and poorer habitats for aquatic life.
- Dams **fragment rivers**, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for **spawning**.
- Reservoirs on floodplains **submerge** the existing vegetation and soil, leading to their decomposition.
- They caused **social movements** like the **Narmada Bachao Andolan** and the **Tehri Dam Andolan**, mainly due to the large-scale **displacement** of local communities, who often gave up their land and livelihood for the greater good of the nation.
- **Inter-state water disputes:** the **Krishna-Godavari dispute** arose from objections by **Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh** to the diversion of more water at **Koyna** by **Maharashtra** for a multipurpose project, which would reduce downstream flow in their states.
- Dams built to control floods have **triggered floods** due to sedimentation in the reservoir; big dams have often failed to control floods during excessive rainfall, and **release of water** from dams during heavy rain has worsened floods.
- Irrigation changed the **cropping pattern** to water-intensive commercial crops, leading to **salinisation** of the soil; and it widened the **social gap** between rich landowners and the landless poor.
- Other problems: earthquakes, water-borne diseases and pests, and pollution from excessive use of water.

blocks.title: Multipurpose projects: benefits and problems
blocks.body:
| Benefits of multipurpose projects | Problems they cause |
|---|---|
| irrigation for agriculture | natural flow of rivers affected; poor sediment flow downstream |
| hydroelectricity | excessive sedimentation at the reservoir bottom; rockier stream beds, poorer aquatic habitats |
| water for homes and industries | rivers fragmented; aquatic fauna cannot migrate to spawn |
| flood control | submerged vegetation and soil decompose; floods triggered by sedimentation and sudden releases |
| recreation, inland navigation, fish breeding | displacement of local people; inter-state disputes; salinisation; widening gap between rich and poor |

blocks.title: Traditional wisdom and modern revival
blocks.body:
Many thought that, given the disadvantages of multipurpose projects, **rainwater harvesting** is a viable alternative, both socio-economically and environmentally. In ancient India, people had in-depth knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types and developed many techniques to harvest **rainwater, groundwater, river water and flood water**, keeping with local ecological conditions.

- In **hill and mountainous regions**, people built diversion channels like the **'guls' or 'kuls'** of the **Western Himalayas** for agriculture.
- **Rooftop rainwater harvesting** was commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in **Rajasthan**.
- In the **floodplains of Bengal**, people developed **inundation channels** to irrigate their fields.
- In **arid and semi-arid regions**, agricultural fields were converted into rain-fed storage structures that allowed the water to stand and moisten the soil, like the **'khadins' in Jaisalmer** and **'johads'** in other parts of Rajasthan.

**Tankas of Rajasthan:** in the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly in **Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer**, almost all houses traditionally had **underground tanks or 'tankas'** for storing drinking water. The tanks could be as large as a big room; one household in **Phalodi** had a tank **6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide**. The tankas were part of a well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system, built inside the main house or the courtyard, and connected to the **sloping roofs** by a pipe. Rain falling on the roofs travelled down the pipe and was stored in the tanka. The **first spell of rain** was usually **not collected**, as it would clean the roofs and pipes. The rainwater stored in tankas is an extremely reliable source of drinking water when all other sources are dried up, and is considered the purest form of natural water, called **'palar pani'**. Many houses built underground rooms adjoining the tanka to beat the summer heat, since it kept the room **cool**. Today the practice is declining in western Rajasthan as perennial water from the **Indira Gandhi Canal** has become available, though some households still maintain tankas because they do not like the taste of tap water.

**Modern revival:**
- **Gendathur**, a remote village in **Mysuru, Karnataka**: villagers have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting in nearly **200 households**, and the village is known for being rich in rainwater.
- **Shillong, Meghalaya**: though Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, about 55 km away, receive the highest rainfall in the world, the city faces acute water shortage; nearly every household has rooftop harvesting, meeting about **15-25 per cent** of its total water requirement.
- **Tamil Nadu** is the **first state in India** to make **rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory** for all houses across the state, with legal provisions to punish defaulters.
- **Bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya:** a **200-year-old** system in which water from streams and springs is tapped by **bamboo pipes**. About **18-20 litres** of water enter the bamboo pipe system per minute and are carried over hundreds of metres, finally reduced to **20-80 drops per minute** at the site of the plant.
- **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (2015):** a central scheme to extend irrigation to every farm ('**Har Khet Ko Pani**') and improve water-use efficiency ('**More crop per drop**') through better irrigation and water conservation.

blocks.title: Traditional water harvesting across India
blocks.body:
| Region | Traditional method |
|---|---|
| Western Himalayas (hills) | **guls or kuls**: diversion channels for agriculture |
| Rajasthan (houses) | **rooftop rainwater harvesting** for drinking water |
| Floodplains of Bengal | **inundation channels** to irrigate fields |
| Arid Rajasthan (Jaisalmer and other parts) | **khadins** and **johads**: fields turned into rain-fed storage |
| Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer | **tankas**: underground tanks storing **palar pani** |
| Meghalaya | **bamboo drip irrigation**, about 200 years old |

blocks.question: Which state first made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses?
blocks.explanation: Tamil Nadu made it compulsory with penalties for defaulters (2025-26 sample paper).
option_feedback: Gendathur village is in Karnataka, but the law is Tamil Nadu's.
Meghalaya has bamboo drip irrigation and Shillong's rooftop harvesting.

blocks.question: What is 'palar pani'?
options: Water from the Indira Gandhi Canal
Rainwater stored in tankas, considered the purest form of natural water
blocks.explanation: Palar pani is stored in the underground tankas of Rajasthan.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Water shares: "96.5 sea, 2.5 sweet"**; of the sweet water, 70% ice, under 30% groundwater.
- **Two model projects: "Bhakra = Bijli + Bhumi (power + irrigation); Hirakud = Holds floods"**.
- **Dams on the map, north to south: "Sally Bought Ten Red Shirts, Her Nephew Took"** = Salal, Bhakra Nangal, Tehri, Rana Pratap Sagar, Sardar Sarovar, Hirakud, Nagarjuna Sagar, Tungabhadra.
- **Harvesting by region:** Himalaya = guls/kuls; Bengal = inundation channels; Rajasthan = khadins, johads, tankas; Meghalaya = bamboo drip.
- **Tamil Nadu = first to make rooftop harvesting compulsory.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying water scarcity happens only where there is no rain: it also comes from **over-use, unequal access and pollution**.
2. Mixing up Bhakra Nangal (**Sutlej**, power and irrigation) and Hirakud (**Mahanadi**, flood control).
3. Saying the first spell of rain is stored in tankas: it is **not collected**; it cleans the roofs and pipes.
4. Placing Sardar Sarovar on the Mahanadi: it is on the **Narmada** in Gujarat.
5. Saying Rajasthan made rooftop harvesting compulsory: it was **Tamil Nadu**.
6. Saying the Krishna-Godavari dispute was about the Narmada: it was about **Maharashtra's diversion at Koyna**, opposed by Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Measure the school roof area and the yearly rainfall of your town, and calculate how many litres the roof could harvest (area in sq m × rainfall in mm = litres). Then let students mark the eight dams on an outline map of India with their rivers.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India', while people displaced by them protested. Write one argument for big dams and one for rainwater harvesting, and say which suits your region better.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 1:** over-irrigation causes waterlogging and salinity.
- **Chapter 2:** dams like Narmada Sagar submerge forests.
- **Chapter 4 (Agriculture):** irrigation and cropping patterns.
- **Chapter 5 (Energy):** hydroelectricity from multipurpose projects.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Multipurpose river projects are both a boon and a curse.' Explain in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Multipurpose projects like Bhakra Nangal and Hirakud provide irrigation, hydroelectricity, water for homes and industries, flood control, navigation, fish breeding and recreation, so Nehru called dams the temples of modern India. But they also block the natural flow of rivers, cause sedimentation and rockier stream beds, fragment rivers so fish cannot migrate to spawn, and submerge forests and soil. They displace local people, as protested by the Narmada Bachao Andolan, and cause inter-state disputes like the Krishna-Godavari one. Sometimes they even trigger floods through sedimentation and sudden releases, and water-intensive crops lead to salinisation. So we must weigh their benefits against their costs and combine them with rainwater harvesting.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Only about 2.5% of the world's water is freshwater; scarcity is caused by population, irrigation, groundwater over-use, industry, cities, unequal access and pollution.
- India had ancient hydraulic structures: Sringaverapura (1st century BC), Bhopal Lake (11th century) and Hauz Khas tank (14th century, Iltutmish).
- Multipurpose projects (Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud) serve many uses but cause ecological damage, displacement, disputes and floods.
- Traditional rainwater harvesting: guls/kuls, rooftop harvesting, inundation channels, khadins, johads, tankas; bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
- Modern efforts: Gendathur, Shillong, Tamil Nadu's compulsory rooftop harvesting and PMKSY (2015).

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper asked which state made rooftop harvesting compulsory (Tamil Nadu), the goal of PMKSY (better irrigation and sustainable water conservation for farmers), and to locate Bhakra Nangal or Hirakud on the map.
- 3/5-mark favourites: causes of water scarcity, benefits and problems of multipurpose projects, rainwater harvesting in Rajasthan and Meghalaya.
- **Map work:** locate Salal, Bhakra Nangal, Tehri, Rana Pratap Sagar, Sardar Sarovar, Hirakud, Nagarjuna Sagar and Tungabhadra.

blocks.back: Underground tanks in Rajasthan (Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer) storing rooftop rainwater (palar pani).

blocks.front: Name two uses each of Bhakra Nangal and Hirakud.
blocks.back: Bhakra Nangal: hydel power and irrigation. Hirakud: water conservation and flood control.

blocks.front: What did the Narmada Bachao Andolan oppose?
blocks.back: The Sardar Sarovar dam: first its environmental damage, later the poor rehabilitation of displaced people.

blocks.front: How does bamboo drip irrigation work?
blocks.back: Bamboo pipes carry 18-20 litres a minute from springs; it is reduced to 20-80 drops a minute at the plant.
